messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 58

# The Body Remembers

Tariq is forty-one years old, and he moves through the world the way water moves around stone — carefully, finding the path of least resistance, always aware of what might break him open. He has been a professional dancer for nearly two decades, first in Beirut and now in a mid-sized American city where he teaches contemporary movement and occasionally performs with a small company. His wife, Dina, is the one who finally persuaded him to come in. She told the intake coordinator that her husband hadn't slept a full night in three years.

The shelling started on a Tuesday. Tariq remembers this with a precision that surprises him — the day of the week, the color of the light, the fact that he had just finished rehearsal and was eating a late lunch with two other dancers when the first impact shook the building. What followed was eleven days that he describes, quietly and without drama, as "the days I stopped being the person I was before." His neighborhood in Beirut was hit repeatedly. He sheltered in a basement with his wife, his elderly mother, and fourteen neighbors. One of those neighbors, a young man named Sami who had been Tariq's student, was killed on the sixth day while trying to retrieve medication from the floor above. Tariq did not see it happen, but he heard it, and he has been hearing it ever since.

He and Dina eventually evacuated. His mother survived. They built a life in the United States, and on the surface that life looks intact — the apartment, the studio, the students who adore him, the marriage that has held. But Tariq knows, and Dina knows, that something fundamental did not make the journey with them.

He cannot watch news footage of any conflict without his chest seizing into a tightness he can only describe as being buried alive. He avoids the news entirely now, which means he sometimes feels cut off from the world, a stranger to conversations his colleagues take for granted. Thunderstorms send him to the interior room of the apartment, sitting on the floor with his back against the wall, waiting for something he cannot name. He does not tell his students this.

What troubles him most — what he returns to again and again in session — is what the trauma has done to his relationship with his own body. Dance has always been the place where he felt most fully himself, most honest, most free. Now there are moments in rehearsal when a particular combination of movement and music will trigger something, and he finds himself suddenly not in the studio but in that basement, smelling concrete dust and fear sweat, hearing Sami's name being called by voices that understood too late. He freezes. He has learned to disguise these moments as artistic pauses, as deliberate stillness, but inside he is somewhere else entirely, and it takes him several minutes to find his way back to the room.

He sleeps in fragments. He wakes at three or four in the morning with his heart already running, already convinced something is wrong, and he lies in the dark cataloguing the sounds of the apartment building until he can persuade himself that each one is ordinary. Dina has learned not to touch him when he wakes this way. Early on she would reach for him, and he would flinch so hard she would cry. He hates that he did that. He mentions it often — not the waking, but the flinching, and what it cost her.

Tariq is not a man who uses the language of damage easily. He speaks about his experience with a kind of careful dignity, choosing words the way he once chose movements — for precision, for truth, for what they reveal rather than conceal. What he says, when he finally says it plainly, is this: he used to live inside his body like it was home. Now he lives inside it like it is a place he is not sure he is allowed to stay.
